section.title: The Temple Completed and Dedicated
section.sectionRationale: Darius searches the archives, finds Cyrus's original decree, and not only confirms it but orders the very enemies of the Jews to fund and protect the work. The temple is finished, dedicated with joy, and the returned exiles keep the Passover, purified and separated to seek the LORD. It is the climax of the first half of Ezra: the house of God completed against all opposition, entirely by the hand of God.
section.thesis: God overrules the empire and its officials to fund, protect, and complete His house, so that opposition ends in provision and the dedication and Passover are kept with a joy that testifies the LORD Himself turned the heart of the king and finished the work.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Darius's decree confirming and funding the work, verses 1 to 12; the temple finished, verses 13 to 15; the joyful dedication, verses 16 to 18; and the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread kept with joy, verses 19 to 22.

units.label: The decree of Darius
units.note: leave this work alone; pay its full cost

verses.text: Thus King Darius ordered a search of the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon.
And a scroll was found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media, with the following written on it: Memorandum:

In the first year of King Cyrus, he issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide,
with three layers of cut stones and one of timbers. The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury.

Furthermore, the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God.
Therefore Darius decreed: To Tattenai governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates and officials in the region: You must stay away from that place!
Leave this work on the house of God alone. Let the governor and elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its original site.

I hereby decree what you must do for these elders of the Jews who are rebuilding this house of God: The cost is to be paid in full to these men from the royal treasury out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates, so that the work will not be hindered.

Whatever is needed, young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil, as requested by the priests in Jerusalem, must be given to them daily without fail.
Then they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons.

I also decree that if any man interferes with this directive, a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it. And his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense.

May God, who has caused His {{shem|Name}} to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued the decree. Let it be carried out with diligence.

units.label: The temple finished
units.note: completed in the sixth year of Darius

verses.text: In response, Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed.

So the Jewish elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished building according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia.
And this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius.

units.label: The joyful dedication
units.note: a sin offering for all Israel

verses.text: Then the people of Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the exiles, celebrated the {{chanukkah|dedication}} of the house of God with joy.
For the dedication of the house of God they offered a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and a sin offering for all Israel of twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel.
They also appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups to the service of God in Jerusalem, according to what is written in the Book of Moses.

units.label: The Passover kept with joy
units.note: the LORD had made them joyful

verses.text: On the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles kept the {{pesach|Passover}}.
All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean. And the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves.
The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had {{badal|separated}} themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel.

For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel.

shem.gloss: Name. Darius's decree speaks of the God who has caused His Name to dwell in Jerusalem, echoing the Old Testament theology of the temple as the place of God's Name, His revealed presence and ownership. Even a pagan king acknowledges that this house belongs to the God whose Name is there.

chanukkah.gloss: Dedication, the setting apart of the completed house for God's service; the same root later gives its name to the Feast of Dedication, Hanukkah. Here the word marks the joyful consecration of the finished temple, a house begun in tears now given wholly to the LORD.

pesach.gloss: Passover, the feast commemorating Israel's redemption from Egypt when the destroyer passed over the blood-marked homes. Kept here by the restored community, from the Hebrew section that resumes at 6:19, it frames the whole return as a new exodus and points to Christ, our Passover Lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7.

badal.gloss: To separate, divide, set apart. Those who ate the Passover were the returned exiles together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the surrounding peoples to seek the LORD. The word marks holiness as consecration to God, and it graciously includes outsiders who turned to seek Him.

basic.context: King Darius orders a search and finds Cyrus's original decree authorizing the temple. He confirms it and goes further: he commands Tattenai and the officials to stop opposing the work, to pay its full cost from the royal treasury, and even to supply the animals and provisions for the sacrifices. The temple is finished in Darius's sixth year, and the people dedicate it with joy, offering a sin offering for all twelve tribes. Then they keep the Passover, purified and separated to seek the LORD, full of joy because God had turned the king's heart. The question is: who finished this house? The LORD did, by ruling kings and reversing His enemies' plans.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the triumphant conclusion of the first half of the book, told as history with a strong theme of God's sovereignty. The great reversal, enemies forced to fund the temple, is meant to make us marvel at God's providence, not to promise that opposition always ends this way. The Passover and dedication are fulfilled in Christ, so we celebrate their meaning rather than repeating their rituals.
basic.originalLanguages: Even Darius confesses the God who caused His Name, His shem, to dwell in Jerusalem. The finished house is set apart in joyful chanukkah, dedication. Then the people keep the pesach, the Passover, and eat it with all who had badal, separated themselves, from uncleanness to seek the LORD.
basic.typology: The completed temple points to Christ, the true dwelling of God with man. The Passover lamb points to Christ, our Passover, sacrificed for us. And the sin offering for all Israel points to the one sacrifice that covers the whole people of God.
basic.christ: The temple is finished, and its whole purpose, God dwelling with His people, is fulfilled in Jesus, in whom all the fullness of God dwells and who is the true meeting place of God and man. The Passover the exiles kept looks straight to Christ, our Passover Lamb, whose blood causes judgment to pass over us. And the joy of the dedication foreshadows the joy of the finished work of salvation.
basic.god: God is gloriously sovereign. He turns the heart of the king, reverses the schemes of enemies so that they must pay for the very house they opposed, and completes what He began. He is the God whose Name dwells among His people, and who makes them joyful.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 5:7 names Christ as our Passover, sacrificed for us. Proverbs 21:1 says God turns the king's heart wherever He wills. And John 2:19-21 shows Christ as the true temple.
basic.oneStory: The first half of Ezra ends in triumph: the house of God is finished, dedicated with joy, and crowned with the Passover, all because God ruled kings and reversed His enemies. It points to the greater house and the greater Passover in Christ, and to the final joy of God dwelling with His people forever.

context.literary: The chapter's first and longest movement, Darius's decree, verses 1 to 12, is a document nested inside a document, an official quotes an old memorandum of Cyrus's, which the king then ratifies and extends with fresh provisions of his own, funding, supplies, and finally a curse on anyone who interferes, closing with the kind of severe formula ancient decrees regularly used to guarantee their own permanence, a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it, verse 11. That severity is not random, it answers, almost word for word, the threat raised in the previous chapter's hostile letter, which warned that a rebuilt Jerusalem would mean the royal treasury will suffer, Ezra 4:13; here the same phrase, royal treasury, reappears, only now commanded to pay the builders' costs in full, verse 8, so that the narrator crafts Darius's decree as a direct, almost gleeful literary reversal of the accusation that opened the opposition two chapters earlier. The remaining three movements move quickly and joyfully, the work's completion is reported in a single date stamped sentence, verse 15, the dedication in a compressed list of sacrifices, verses 16 to 18, and the Passover in a final scene of purified worship, verses 19 to 22. At verse 19 the text shifts from Aramaic back into Hebrew, and that linguistic homecoming enacts, in the very texture of the book's language, the community's own homecoming from imperial documents and foreign courts back into the native rhythms of covenant feasts.
context.historical: The temple's completion on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius, verse 15, works out to around 516 BC, some seventy years after the first temple's destruction in 586 BC, a span that let Ezra's first readers hear a fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy that Babylon's desolation of the land would last seventy years, Jeremiah 25:11 to 12, 29:10. The scroll authorizing all this turns up not in Babylon but in the fortress of Ecbatana in Media, verse 2, the Persian kings' summer residence in the mountains, a detail consistent with the empire's practice of moving between several capitals through the year and filing state records wherever the court happened to be sitting when a decree was issued. Persian kings were known more broadly for financing and restoring the cults of peoples they had conquered rather than suppressing them, a policy consistent with Cyrus's own inscriptions describing himself as a restorer of local sanctuaries and returner of displaced peoples to their homes, which lends outside plausibility to a Persian king funding, supplying, and legally protecting a foreign people's temple exactly as Ezra 6 describes. The dedication offerings, a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve goats, verse 17, while generous for a small returned community, are modest next to Solomon's original dedication, where twenty two thousand oxen and a hundred twenty thousand sheep were sacrificed, 1 Kings 8:63, a quiet reminder that this second house, however joyfully consecrated, was still the house Haggai calls a day of small things.
context.canonical: The twelve male goats offered for all Israel, one for each tribe, verse 17, deliberately recall the dedication of the tabernacle in the wilderness, where each of the twelve tribal leaders brought an identical offering over twelve days, Numbers 7:12 to 83, and reassert, centuries later and with only a fraction of the tribes physically present, that the whole nation, including those still scattered among the nations, remains one people before God, a hope that later becomes explicit when Ezekiel pictures the two divided kingdoms joined again into a single stick in the prophet's hand, Ezekiel 37:15 to 22. This Passover also joins a small but significant trilogy of restoration Passovers scattered through Israel's history, Hezekiah summons a scattered, compromised nation to keep a late but joyful Passover after generations of neglect, 2 Chronicles 30, Josiah's reforming generation keeps one so faithfully that the record says no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges, 2 Kings 23:21 to 23, and now the returned exiles keep a third, each marking a fresh beginning in covenant life after a season of failure or exile. And the completion itself, arriving after the discouragement of chapters 4 and 5, answers in part the promise Haggai had spoken only months earlier, that the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, Haggai 2:9, even though the modest scale of the dedication shows that promise still awaits its fuller answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Having spent two chapters narrating opposition, delay, and a forced standstill, the author now wants his reader to feel the full weight of reversal, the very machinery that had been used against God's people, imperial decree, royal archive, provincial governor, is turned, without any change of empire or ruler, into the machinery that finishes and funds God's house. His intent is not to promise that every act of opposition will end with the opposition paying for what it once tried to stop, but to press home that no earthly power operates outside God's authority to redirect it. He also wants the community's worship at the end, marked repeatedly by joy, to be read against the tears of chapter 3's foundation, the same generation, or their children, who once could not tell weeping from shouting now dedicate a finished house purely in joy, showing that grief over a small beginning is not the final word on how the story ends.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter records one particular, historically remarkable reversal of one empire's policy; it does not promise believers that governments will always fund or protect what they once opposed, and Scripture elsewhere shows faithful obedience meeting no such favorable outcome at all, from Daniel's friends in the furnace to believers under later persecuting emperors. Likewise the Passover, the sin offering, and the ceremonial purification of priests described here belong to a sacrificial system Christ has fulfilled once for all, so the church does not slaughter lambs or offer sin offerings for the twelve tribes. What does transfer is the pattern of faith the chapter displays, separating from what is unclean in order to seek the LORD, verse 21, receiving whatever provision comes, whether scant or abundant, as from God's hand rather than mere circumstance, and offering joy, not grudging relief, when a long delayed work is finally finished.

debates.question: Why did God allow years of opposition, only for it to end in the empire funding the temple?

views.label: God turns opposition into greater blessing
views.case: The reversal, enemies compelled to pay for the house they fought, displays God's sovereign power and shames the opposition; the delay set the stage for a triumph no one could credit to human strength, magnifying the LORD who rules kings' hearts.

views.label: God's timing trains and completes
views.case: The pause coincided with the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah and taught the people dependence; God finished the work in His own appointed time, so that the completion answered His word rather than mere circumstance.

debates.bearing: Both readings exalt God's providence: behind a frowning providence He hid a smiling face, weaving even fierce opposition into the completion and funding of His house.

debates.question: Why offer a sin offering of twelve goats for all Israel when only some tribes had returned?

views.label: Representing the whole covenant people
views.case: The twelve goats confess that Israel is one people of twelve tribes before God, even when scattered; the returned remnant offers atonement on behalf of the entire nation, refusing to write off the exiles who had not come home.

views.label: Hope for a full restoration
views.case: The number twelve voices an eschatological hope that God will yet gather all His people; the offering looks beyond the small remnant to the complete Israel God intends to save, a hope realized in Christ.

debates.bearing: Either way, the offering testifies to one undivided people of God, a unity finally secured in Christ, who gathers all His own, Jew and Gentile, into one body.

study.originalLanguages: Four further terms deepen the chapter's testimony. Darius's decree says God has caused his Name to dwell there, verse 12, using a form of the same root that lies behind mishkan, tabernacle, and the verb to dwell or settle, the root bound up with the whole theology of a portable, then permanent, dwelling place for God among his people, Exodus 25:8; remarkably, it is a pagan king's own chancery Aramaic that preserves this deeply Israelite theological vocabulary, testifying, however unintentionally, that even Persia's records recognized this house as belonging to a God who dwells, not merely visits. The curse Darius attaches to anyone who tampers with his decree is unusually vivid, the offender's house is to become a dunghill or refuse heap, a term used elsewhere for utter degradation and disgrace, so that the punishment for obstructing God's house is imagined as the total reversal of a household's honor, turned from a place of habitation into a heap of waste. The dimensions specified for the house, sixty cubits high and sixty wide, verse 3, preserve a textual puzzle worth noting on its own terms, some ancient versions read a different figure closer to Solomon's own measurements, sixty long, twenty wide, thirty high, compare 1 Kings 6:2, a reminder that the memorandum quoted here reaches the reader through a chain of copying and translation even within the story's own world. Once the narrative shifts back into Hebrew at verse 19, its central sacrificial term is the standard word for sin offering, the offering that dealt with the community's guilt rather than merely expressing thanksgiving, distinguishing the twelve goats of the dedication from the burnt offerings and freewill gifts named earlier in the book. And the word for separate, badal, which marks those who joined the Passover after separating themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land, is the same verb God uses when he tells Israel at Sinai, I have separated you from the peoples to be mine, Leviticus 20:26, using it here for anyone, presumably including some from the surrounding population, who turned to seek the LORD, shows that the line the word draws was never about ancestry alone but about a decisive turning toward Israel's God, open in principle to whoever crossed it.

typology.type: The completed temple where God's Name dwells
typology.fulfillment: The completed temple, filled with sacrifice and song after years of tears and delay, existed for one purpose beyond any other, to be the place where God's Name, his manifest presence, dwelt among his people. Paul says that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9, and Jesus himself, standing in a later version of this very building, calls his own body the true temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days, John 2:19 to 21. The type reaches its limit in scale, stone walls housed God's presence in one city, while the risen Christ makes his dwelling available to anyone, anywhere, who comes to him.

typology.type: The Passover lamb kept by the exiles
typology.fulfillment: The Passover the exiles kept, purified and separated to seek the LORD, remembered a lamb whose blood once turned aside the destroyer in Egypt, Exodus 12:13. John the Baptist recognizes the pattern completed in a person rather than an animal, calling Jesus the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29, and Paul states the equation directly, Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The type escalates from covering one household behind blood on a doorframe to covering, in principle, every nation under Christ's blood, and from a meal repeated yearly to a sacrifice offered only once.

typology.type: The sin offering for all twelve tribes
typology.fulfillment: Twelve goats for twelve tribes, offered together as one sin offering, pictured the whole covenant people as a single body needing one atonement, even though only a remnant had actually returned to offer it. Hebrews contrasts this and every other repeated offering with Christ, who offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins and by it has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified, Hebrews 10:12, 14, a sacrifice large enough to gather a multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The twelve goats could only symbolize a scattered nation's unity, Christ's one offering actually achieves it, across every nation, not only Israel's tribes.

study.christ: Darius's astonishing turnaround, an emperor commanding his own treasury to fund the very house his officials had tried to stop, previews on a small, regional stage what Christ claims on a cosmic one. Where a single Persian king's heart was turned to serve the building of one temple in one province, the risen Christ says all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me, Matthew 28:18, so that every throne, not one, now exists to serve the spread of his kingdom, whether its occupants know it or not, exactly as Darius unknowingly served a purpose far larger than his own administration. The phrase repeated throughout these chapters, the God of heaven, quietly narrows the distance between an exiled people's confession and Christ's own claim, a title once used to distinguish Israel's God from Persia's many gods becomes, in Jesus's mouth, a claim of shared authority over both realms his title names. The chapter's insistence that the LORD had made them joyful, verse 22, also answers something Paul will later promise every believer in unfinished, ongoing form, he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ, Philippians 1:6. The exiles' temple, begun in fear and tears, Ezra 3:12, and finished in joy, Ezra 6:16, is a small, complete rehearsal of what every believer can expect writ large across a whole lifetime, that the God who starts a work of grace does not abandon it half built the way Jesus warns an undercapitalized builder might, Luke 14:28 to 30. And the sacrifices offered at the dedication, though real and costly, could still only cover sin for a time; Christ's finished work needed no annual, or even generational, repetition, so that the joy Ezra records at one temple's completion is a shadow of the far greater and final joy of a salvation that, once finished at the cross, never needs finishing again.
study.god: There is a kind of poetic justice in how God governs this chapter that borders on holy irony, the very officials who had accused Jerusalem of threatening the royal treasury, Ezra 4:13, are the ones Darius now commands to empty that treasury on the temple's behalf, and the very archive search the enemies wanted used against the Jews, Ezra 4:15, becomes, instead, the archive search that vindicates them, Ezra 6:1 to 2. God does not merely overcome opposition, he redirects it so that it serves the opposite of what it intended, a pattern that shows his sovereignty operating with something like wit as well as power. He is also meticulous about the details of worship, not only its grand occasions, the priests and Levites purified themselves and were ceremonially clean before a single lamb was slaughtered, verse 20, showing that the God who finishes the whole project is equally concerned with the smaller, unglamorous preparations that make right worship possible, and that a completed building means little without a properly prepared priesthood to serve in it. His faithfulness spans a timescale longer than most human patience can hold, roughly seventy years from Jerusalem's fall to the temple's completion, and closer to twenty years from the first decree of Cyrus to this final dedication, a reminder that his promises are not measured against a single generation's expectations but against his own timing, which he keeps exactly. And the note that closes the chapter, the LORD had made them joyful, credits their gladness not to circumstance but to God himself as its direct source, distinguishing this joy from mere relief that a long project was finally over, it is the specific gift of a God who delights to make his people glad, not only to finish his own work but to let them feel the completion of it. Every part of this chapter, decree, archive, sacrifice, feast, answers finally to him alone.

crossReferences.note: Paul declares that Christ our Passover lamb has already been sacrificed and calls believers to keep the feast not with the old leaven of malice but with sincerity and truth, showing that the Passover the exiles kept in verse 19 finds its true fulfillment and its ongoing ethical shape in the Lord's Supper and the whole Christian life.

Solomon teaches that the king's heart is like a stream of water in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he pleases, the exact mechanism behind Darius's reversal in this chapter, where an emperor who could have crushed the project instead becomes its chief funder and protector.

Jesus tells the temple authorities to destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, and John explains that he spoke of the temple of his body, so that the completed house of Ezra 6, however joyfully dedicated, was never more than a signpost toward the true and final dwelling of God with humanity.

Only months before this chapter's events, Haggai promised that the glory of this very house would exceed the glory of Solomon's, a promise not fully answered by stone or gold but by the greater one who would one day walk its courts and outshine every temple built by human hands.

Jeremiah's prophecy that after seventy years in Babylon the LORD would fulfill his promise and bring the exiles back finds its precise historical answer in the roughly seventy years between the first temple's destruction and this second temple's completion in the sixth year of Darius.

At the tabernacle's own dedication each of Israel's twelve tribal leaders brought an identical offering over twelve days, establishing the pattern of twelve equal offerings for a united nation that the twelve goats of Ezra 6:17 deliberately echo at this later, much smaller dedication.

Josiah's Passover is remembered as unmatched since the days of the judges, part of a small cluster of restoration Passovers, alongside Hezekiah's and this one kept by the returned exiles, each marking a fresh national turning back to covenant faithfulness after a season of failure.

Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth, the full and final version of the authority a single Persian king exercises in this chapter over one province and one building project, showing every earthly throne as a shadow of the dominion Christ alone truly holds.

Paul assures believers that God, who began a good work in them, will bring it to completion by the day of Christ, the same confident pattern this chapter displays on a national scale, a work begun in tears at the foundation and finished, exactly as promised, in joy.

Paul writes that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, the ultimate answer to Darius's own acknowledgment that God had caused his Name to dwell in the Jerusalem temple this chapter completes and dedicates.

study.oneStory: Scripture keeps marking its greatest turning points with the single word finished. Creation itself closes with God resting because the heavens and the earth were finished, Genesis 2:1, the tabernacle is finished by Moses and immediately filled with glory, Exodus 40:33 to 34, Solomon finishes the first temple and the glory of the LORD fills it so thickly the priests cannot stand to minister, 1 Kings 8:10 to 11, and now, on a far smaller scale, this second temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius and greeted with its own more modest, but no less real, filling of dedication and joy. Ezra 6 stands in that long procession as a humbler but genuine link, proof that God had not forgotten how to finish what he starts even after judgment, exile, and decades of delay. The chapter's twin center pieces, the joyful dedication and the kept Passover, gather up the whole architecture of the story so far, the temple answers the ache of Eden lost, a place where God dwells with his people again, however partially, and the Passover answers the ache of bondage, the reminder that this people exists at all because a lamb's blood once turned aside a deserved judgment, Exodus 12:13. Both institutions, temple and Passover, converge completely in Jesus, who does not merely finish another building or repeat another feast but announces from the cross the very word this whole pattern has been waiting for, it is finished, John 19:30, the sacrifice that ends every future need for lambs, sin offerings, or rebuilt houses. And the same word will be spoken once more at the very end of the story, when a voice from the throne declares over the new heaven and new earth, it is done, Revelation 21:6, the temple no longer a building at all but God and the Lamb dwelling directly with a people who need no other light.

quiz.q: What did Darius do after Cyrus's decree was found in the archives?

options.text: He confirmed it and ordered the officials to fund the work fully and stop opposing it.
options.note: Verses 6-12 record Darius confirming the decree and commanding full support.

options.text: He cancelled the project as too expensive.
options.note: The opposite: he ordered it funded from the royal treasury.

options.text: He ignored the decree and did nothing.
options.note: He acted decisively to confirm and enforce it.

options.text: He ordered the temple destroyed.
options.note: He protected the temple and threatened those who would harm it.

quiz.q: What is remarkable about who ended up paying for the temple?

options.text: The enemies who had opposed the work were commanded to fund and supply it.
options.note: God reversed the opposition so the officials paid for the very house they resisted.

options.text: The Jews alone paid for everything themselves.
options.note: The people gave, but Darius ordered the royal treasury to pay the full cost.

options.text: No money was needed at all.
options.note: Real funding was required, and Darius decreed it be paid in full.

options.text: A foreign army seized the funds by force.
options.note: The funds came by royal decree, not by force.

quiz.q: How did the people respond when the temple was completed?

options.text: They dedicated the house of God with joy and kept the Passover.
options.note: Verses 16-22 describe the joyful dedication and the Passover.

options.text: They mourned that it was not as grand as Solomon's.
options.note: That was the earlier reaction at the foundation; here the note is joy.

options.text: They immediately abandoned it and returned to Babylon.
options.note: They stayed, worshiped, and celebrated with joy.

options.text: They argued over who should be high priest.
options.note: The chapter records joyful, ordered worship, not dispute.

quiz.q: Who does the text say was ultimately behind the temple's completion?

options.text: The LORD, who turned the king's heart and made His people joyful.
options.note: Verse 22 credits the LORD with turning the king's heart to strengthen their hands.

options.text: The skill of the Jewish builders alone.
options.note: Human effort was real, but the text credits God's sovereign hand.

options.text: The generosity of Tattenai the governor.
options.note: Tattenai obeyed Darius; the LORD is named as the true cause.

options.text: Good luck and favorable timing.
options.note: The text names God's providence, not luck.

quiz.q: How does the exiles' Passover point to Christ?

options.text: The Passover lamb foreshadows Christ, our Passover, sacrificed so that judgment passes over us.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 5:7 makes Christ the fulfillment of the Passover.

options.text: It teaches that we must keep the Passover ritual to be saved.
options.note: The feast is fulfilled in Christ; we celebrate its meaning, not repeat the ritual for salvation.

options.text: It shows the exiles no longer needed sacrifice.
options.note: They kept the Passover sacrifice, which pointed forward to Christ's.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The Passover points directly to Christ, our Passover Lamb.

questions: God turned the plans of the enemies into provision for His house. Where do you need to trust that God can reverse opposition and even make it serve His purposes?
The people dedicated the finished house with joy after years of delay and tears. How does remembering that God completes what He begins encourage you in an unfinished, discouraging work?

Those who ate the Passover had separated themselves from uncleanness to seek the LORD, and outsiders who turned to God were welcomed too. What might holy separation to seek God, without proud exclusion, look like for you?
The whole point of the temple was God dwelling with His people, fulfilled in Christ. How does knowing that God dwells with you in Jesus shape your daily life?
The text says the LORD had made them joyful. Where is your joy resting on circumstances rather than on the God who finishes His work, and how might that change?

translationNotes.note: The dimensions sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide are unusual; the BSB footnote notes a Syriac reading closer to Solomon's temple, sixty long, twenty wide, thirty high. The figures come from the Persian memorandum.
The temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius, 516 BC, close to seventy years after its destruction, matching Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years.
From this verse the text returns to Hebrew after the long Aramaic section that began at 4:8; the shift accompanies the move from imperial documents back to Israel's covenant worship.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ezra 6:1-22. Words drawn from 6:1-18 are marked Aramaic and from 6:19-22 Hebrew.
